title: Checkpoint: Kings, Parliaments and Law
objective: After this level you can explain how kings, parliaments and courts shared power by 1450.
summary: By 1450 an English king ruled alongside a charter kings kept reconfirming, a Parliament that granted taxes and courts of common law and juries. A timeline from 1166 to 1431 ties the chapter together.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: by the late Middle Ages, England’s king no longer ruled alone.
cards.body: A charter kings kept reconfirming, a Parliament that held the purse strings, and courts of common law and juries. Let’s put the chapter on one page.

cards.headline: Kings, parliaments and law, in order

events.label: Assize of Clarendon: juries name suspects
King John agrees to Magna Carta
Joan of Arc is burned at Rouen

cards.headline: The charter that wouldn’t die
cards.body: Remember Level 71’s flop, annulled within ten weeks? Kings kept confirming it: modern research counts as many as 44 reaffirmations, the last in 1423. In 1297 it was recorded in the Statute Rolls for the first time. By the 14th century, Parliament’s regular reconfirmations were a public reminder that the king had to uphold the rule of law. The king still ruled. He just no longer ruled alone.

mascot.line: Charters, parliaments, juries: you just watched a king pick up company. Nicely done.

cards.headline: Three checks on a crown
cards.body: Put the chapter together and you get three checks. Magna Carta: no free man imprisoned without lawful judgment or the law of the land. Parliament: extra taxes for war needed its agreement. Common law: judges followed earlier decisions, so the law was common to all England, not the whim of the day.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How Magna Carta, Parliament and common law meant England's king no longer ruled alone.
Why kings' need for tax money turned their councils into parliaments that included the towns.
How juries went from naming suspects to deciding guilt once the Church stopped blessing ordeals.
Why England and France fought for over a century, and how longbows won battles but not the war.

questions.prompt: Who presided over the church court that tried Joan of Arc at Rouen?

options.label: Pope Callixtus III, in Rome
options.rationale: He authorised the retrial that cleared her.

options.label: King Henry V of England
options.rationale: He had died before her trial.

options.label: Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais
King Charles VII of France
options.rationale: He was the king she had helped crown.

questions.explanation: The church court at Rouen was led by Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais.

questions.prompt: Magna Carta was annulled in 1215. What shows it still mattered by the 1400s?

options.label: It was never mentioned again after its 1225 reissue
Kings reaffirmed it as many as 44 times, last in 1423
The Pope made it part of Church law for all Europe
options.rationale: Parliament and kings, not popes, kept it alive.

options.label: It replaced common law in all the king’s courts

questions.explanation: Modern research counts as many as 44 reaffirmations, the last in 1423, and Parliament used them to assert the rule of law.

Heavy cannon brought over from England
options.rationale: The story is archers, stakes and mud.

options.label: A surprise attack on the French camp at night
options.rationale: The French advanced into the arrows.

options.label: Sharpened stakes and a narrow, muddy field

questions.explanation: The English stood on a ploughed field narrowed by woods, behind stakes, while the French struggled through mud.

questions.prompt: Kings and law in 1215: besides Magna Carta, what legal turning point came that year?

options.label: Parliament met for the very first time
options.rationale: The word parliament first appears in 1236.

options.label: Trial by combat was abolished
The Church withdrew priests from trials by ordeal
Juries were invented by the Pope

questions.explanation: The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 forbade priests to bless ordeals, and England turned to juries.
